overview: Ryazan’s principality continued after its old capital’s destruction in 1237, with Pereyaslavl Ryazansky becoming its later centre. Moscow absorbed it in 1521. Archaeology reveals crafts, homes and children’s games. The imported map outline is grossly overbroad and should not be read as a reliable historical boundary.

periods.title: The old capital flourishes
periods.summary: Old Ryazan developed as a capital with stone churches and substantial craft quarters.

periods.title: A principality after catastrophe
periods.summary: Survivors attempted to rebuild Old Ryazan; Pereyaslavl became the later political centre.

periods.title: Later Ryazan
periods.summary: The principality survived until its incorporation into the Muscovite state in 1521.

sections.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan

items.text: At excavation 47 in Old Ryazan, archaeologists uncovered two neighbouring properties with houses, workshops and outbuildings. Collapsed clay ovens mark where households heated rooms and cooked. The remains place paid craftwork close to domestic life: going to work might mean crossing the yard rather than travelling across town.

One property contained bronze dies for shaping silver ornaments, along with parts of scales, small weights, tweezers and spilled metal. Together these finds identify jewellery production more securely than a single lost earring would. One die carried a centaur with sword and shield, a tiny warrior ready for repeated impressions.

An excavated pit beneath a dwelling is identified by the researchers as a cellar used for ice storage. Underground storage helped households manage food before electric refrigerators. Its survival adds a practical detail to the same neighbourhood where attractive ornaments were being made.

A bone chess piece from the southern property dates to the late twelfth or first half of the thirteenth century. Its abstract shape belongs to an eastern style of set; two projections may represent an elephant’s tusks. The museum interprets this costly game as evidence of a prosperous household.

The craft neighbourhood also yielded pendants made from Byzantine copper coins and fragments of green-glazed clay toys. The toys resemble southern Rus pottery of the early thirteenth century. Adults’ ornaments and children’s playthings both preserve connections beyond the city, without telling us who personally carried them there.

Gold ornaments uncovered by people working near the old city’s cathedral in 1822 helped draw scholarly attention to Old Ryazan. Another hoard was excavated inside a house oven in 1950. People chose different hiding places for valuables; the objects survived because their owners did not recover them.

A hoard discovered near Isady, about four kilometres east of Old Ryazan, included neck rings, bracelets and silver money ingots. Because it was found outside the city, its setting matters. The excavation team discusses settlements and a possible route to a river landing, rather than assuming every treasure came from the capital’s houses.

The museum’s food summary covers medieval and later deposits from Pereyaslavl, including rye, oats, buckwheat, millet and fish bones. These finds reveal ingredients used across several periods. They cannot all be securely assigned to the independent principality before 1521.

The Vvedensky excavation revealed successive wooden street surfaces, with boards resting on three long pine supports. The museum describes them in its medieval-town account without assigning every layer an exact date. Walking here could sound like footsteps on a wooden floor.

The museum reports bird-shaped whistles, rattles and about thirty pine-bark boats among the Vvedensky finds. It imagines children sailing them on the nearby Lybid. Exact layers are unspecified: these are evidence of the town’s past play, not a precisely dated toy collection.

A thirteenth- or fourteenth-century drawing scratched into birch bark shows a horse and people. It was found during pipe work near the later Vvedensky excavation. Museum researchers interpret its style as a child’s drawing, while identifying some figures only tentatively. A small scrap preserves someone’s view of ordinary movement and company.

A fifteenth-century birch-bark fragment from Pereyaslavl contains the Cyrillic word “невѣриѧ”, literally “unbelief”. This Church Slavonic sample comes from a religious prophecy associated with Easter-date calculations. The scholarly catalogue dates the fragment about 1450 to 1500; it is not a complete message, and the word is shown in the editor’s historical transcription.

ending.text: Moscow incorporated the Ryazan principality in 1521. Its towns and inhabitants continued under new rulers. Old Ryazan’s destruction in 1237 preceded the principality’s final political ending by centuries.
